interview_tips.observation: When asked about the pgvector migration, you jumped straight into the technical details (sync latency, IVFFlat indexing) without first setting the context of the problem and your role.
interview_tips.suggestion: Use the STAR framework: Start with the Situation (Contextual's legal RAG had stale embeddings causing hallucinations), Task (you needed to eliminate sync latency), Action (you led the migration to pgvector after benchmarking), and Result (zero sync latency, matched performance). This makes the story compelling and easy to follow.

interview_tips.observation: You mentioned building consensus with a spreadsheet, but didn't elaborate on the stakeholder dynamics or how you convinced them.
interview_tips.suggestion: For senior roles, 'building consensus' is a key skill. Describe who the stakeholders were (e.g., CTO, product manager, legal team), what their concerns were (cost vs. performance), and how you addressed them. This shows strategic influence.

interview_tips.observation: You didn't explicitly connect your technical work to business outcomes, like converting pilots to paid contracts (which is on your CV).
interview_tips.suggestion: Always tie your technical decisions to business impact. For example: 'By eliminating stale embeddings, we reduced hallucinated citations from 22% to 4%, which was the key metric that convinced our first three enterprise customers to sign.' This positions you as a business-aware engineer.

interview_tips.observation: Your answers were dense and packed with multiple technical points, which can overwhelm the listener.
interview_tips.suggestion: After stating your main point, pause and ask 'Does that make sense?' or 'Would you like me to go deeper on any part of that?' This gives the interviewer control and makes the conversation more interactive.
